title: Implement Queue using Stacks / Stack using Queues.
shortTitle: Implement Queue using Stacks / Stack using Queues
keyPoints: Two stacks make a queue: inbox for enqueue, outbox for dequeue; transfer only when outbox is empty.
One queue makes a stack: after adding the new element, rotate all earlier elements behind it so newest is at front.
The two-stack queue has amortized O(1) per operation; the queue-based stack has O(n) push.
Lazy transfer is critical; eager transfer breaks ordering and amortized complexity.
The two-stack queue is practically useful (Banker's queue); the queue-stack is mostly an exercise.
Stacks and queues are inter-convertible, proving neither is strictly more powerful than the other.

s1_definition.oneliner: Two stacks make a queue by reversing order on lazy transfer; a queue makes a stack by rotating the newest element to the front on every push.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Queue from two stacks** – push to an input stack; dequeue from an output stack, transferring only when the output is empty, for amortized O(1).
- **Stack from one queue** – on push, add the element then rotate all earlier elements behind it, making push O(n) and pop/top O(1).
- **Lazy transfer** – transfer only when the output stack is empty; eager transfer breaks ordering and complexity.
- **Inter-convertibility** – stacks and queues can simulate each other, proving neither is strictly more powerful.
- **Practical use** – the two-stack queue appears as the Banker's queue in functional data structures.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India token counter, a queue is first-come-first-served, but the clerk only has two trays (stacks). When the serving tray is empty, she flips the intake tray into the serving tray, reversing order so the oldest is on top. For the reverse problem, she has a waiting line (queue) and fakes LIFO by rotating the line on every new arrival so the newest is always at the front.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Queue from Two Stacks
  ─────────────────────
  enqueue A, B, C:
  Input: [C,B,A]   Output: []

  dequeue → output empty → transfer:
  Input: []   Output: [A,B,C]
  pop A (FIFO)

  Stack from One Queue
  ─────────────────────
  push A:  queue=[A]
  push B:  queue=[B,A] (rotated)
  push C:  queue=[C,B,A] (rotated)
  pop → C (LIFO)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Two stacks make a queue by lazy transfer: push to an inbox, pour into an outbox only when the outbox is empty, and the reversal gives FIFO order. Each element moves between stacks at most once, giving amortized O(1). One queue makes a stack by rotating all earlier elements behind each new arrival, making push O(n) and pop O(1).

The lazy transfer rule is what makes the two-stack queue efficient. Eager transfer on every dequeue breaks both the ordering and the amortized guarantee. The distinction between worst-case O(n) for one call and amortized O(1) over all operations is the real point interviewers test.

The two-stack queue is practically useful and appears as the Banker's queue in functional data structures. The queue-based stack is mostly an interview exercise because one operation is always linear. Together they prove stacks and queues are inter-convertible.

In my project at the National Bank of India, a constrained teller component used only stack primitives, but customer requests needed FIFO fairness. The two-stack queue delivered correct ordering with amortized O(1) throughput.

Remember one sentence: two stacks make a queue with lazy transfer for amortized O(1), and a queue makes a stack by rotating the newest to the front for O(n) push.
